claim: The distribution of CV* values for the otolith afferent dataset was bimodal (p=0.04, Hartigan's dip test).
source: We found that the distribution of CV* values for our dataset was bimodal (Figure 1B, p=0.04, Hartigan's dip test), consistent with previous studies (reviewed in Goldberg, 2000).
evidence: Statistical test (Hartigan's dip test) was performed on the experimental data showing bimodal distribution with p=0.04.

claim: The otolith afferent dataset comprised N = 18 regular and N = 17 irregular afferents.
source: Our afferent dataset thus comprised N = 18 regular and N = 17 irregular afferents.
evidence: Direct statement of the sample sizes in the experimental dataset.

claim: Irregular afferents displayed greater sensitivity to the stimulus than their regular counterparts.
source: Further analysis of neuronal responses across our dataset revealed that irregular afferents displayed greater sensitivity to the stimulus than their regular counterparts (Figure 1D and Figure 1D, left inset).
evidence: Analysis of neuronal responses across the dataset with reference to Figure 1D showing sensitivity differences.

claim: The residual power spectrum was higher by over an order of magnitude for irregular afferents compared to regular afferents.
source: Further analysis of the residual power spectrum revealed nearly constant power, which was higher by over an order of magnitude for irregular afferents (Figure 1D, right inset, compare red and blue curves).
evidence: Analysis of residual power spectrum from experimental data with reference to Figure 1D.

claim: The square root of the RR coherence was higher for irregular afferents than for regular afferents.
source: Overall, the square root of the RR coherence was higher for irregular afferents than for regular afferents (Figure 2B,C, compare solid red and blue curves), confirming our observation that irregular afferents display lower trial-to-trial variability than their regular counterparts.
evidence: Coherence analysis of experimental data with reference to Figure 2B,C.

claim: The population-averaged nonlinearity index (NI) value was significantly higher for irregular afferents (40.8 ± 2.2%) than for regular afferents (20.0 ± 4.1%; p<0.001).
source: As expected, the population-averaged NI value was significantly higher for irregular afferents (Figure 2D; irregular: 40.8 ± 2.2%, regular: 20.0 ± 4.1%; p<0.001, Wilcoxon ranksum test).
evidence: Statistical comparison of nonlinearity index values between afferent types with Wilcoxon ranksum test.

claim: Irregular afferents transmitted significantly more information (0.37 ± 0.05 bits/spk) than regular afferents (0.24 ± 0.04 bits/spk; p=0.04).
source: Overall, the mutual information rate densities of irregular afferents were consistently higher across frequencies than those of regular afferents (Figure 2E, left panel, compare red and blue curves), leading to significantly greater rates of information transmission (Figure 2E, right panel; irregular: 0.37 ± 0.05 bits/spk; regular: 0.24 ± 0.04 bits/spk; p=0.04, Wilcoxon ranksum test).
evidence: Mutual information analysis with statistical comparison using Wilcoxon ranksum test.

claim: Maximum discrimination performance for irregular afferents was observed for timescales of 10 ms or frequencies of 100 Hz.
source: Importantly, maximum performance for irregular afferents was observed for timescales of 10 ms (Figure 3C) or, equivalently, frequencies of 100 Hz (Figure 3D, red arrow).
evidence: Analysis of discrimination performance across timescales with reference to Figure 3C and 3D.

claim: The frequency at which discrimination performance was maximum for irregular afferents (100 Hz) was five-fold greater than those contained in the naturalistic translational self-motion stimulus (<20 Hz).
source: This frequency was five-fold greater than those contained in the naturalistic translational self-motion stimulus (<20 Hz; shaded gray area).
evidence: Comparison of maximum discrimination frequency to stimulus frequency content.

claim: Discrimination performance for regular afferents reached its maximum value for timescales near 50 ms or frequencies at which there is significant stimulus power (~20 Hz).
source: By contrast, the discrimination performance for regular afferents reached its maximum value for timescales near 50 ms (Figure 3C) or, equivalently, for frequencies at which there is significant stimulus power (~20 Hz; Figure 3D, blue arrow).
evidence: Analysis of discrimination performance for regular afferents with reference to Figure 3C and 3D.

claim: Discrimination performance was strongly positively correlated with resting discharge variability (CV*) (R = 0.89, p<0.001).
source: Discrimination performance (Figure 3E) and spike-timing precision (i.e., the frequency at which discrimination performance is maximum; Figure 3F) were both strongly positively correlated with resting discharge variability, as quantified by CV* (performance: R = 0.89, p<0.001; precision: R = 0.71, p<0.001).
evidence: Correlation analysis between discrimination performance and CV* with statistical significance.

claim: Spike-timing precision was strongly positively correlated with resting discharge variability (CV*) (R = 0.71, p<0.001).
source: Discrimination performance (Figure 3E) and spike-timing precision (i.e., the frequency at which discrimination performance is maximum; Figure 3F) were both strongly positively correlated with resting discharge variability, as quantified by CV* (performance: R = 0.89, p<0.001; precision: R = 0.71, p<0.001).
evidence: Correlation analysis between spike-timing precision and CV* with statistical significance.

claim: The mathematical model reproduced experimental findings by co-varying resting discharge variability and sensitivity parameters such that their ratio remains constant.
source: Overall, we found that, by co-varying the resting discharge variability and sensitivity parameters such that their ratio remains constant (Figure 4A, right panel), which is consistent with previous experimental findings (Jamali et al., 2013), we were able to reproduce the experimental data from regular and irregular afferents with good accuracy (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Model simulation results compared to experimental data with reference to previous findings.

claim: All three phase-locking index (PLI) measures were significantly higher for irregular afferents than for regular afferents (p<0.001 in all cases).
source: Qualitatively similar results were seen across our dataset as all three PLI measures were significantly higher for irregular afferents than for their regular counterparts (Figure 5D, solid bars; p<0.001 in all cases, Wilcoxon ranksum tests).
evidence: Statistical comparison of phase-locking indices between afferent types using Wilcoxon ranksum tests.

claim: Model-predicted PLI values were comparable to those obtained experimentally for both irregular and regular afferents.
source: Furthermore, we simulated our regular and irregular afferent models and found PLI values that were comparable to those obtained experimentally (Figure 5D, compare solid and hollow bars; irregular — p=0.73, p=0.55, and p=1 for PLI1, PLI2, and PLI3, respectively; regular — p=0.83, p=0.50, and p=1 for PLI1, PLI2, and PLI3, respectively; Wilcoxon ranksum tests).
evidence: Comparison of model predictions to experimental data with statistical tests showing no significant differences.

claim: Irregular afferents displayed increased tendency to phase lock with increasing stimulation frequency.
source: Overall, irregular afferents displayed increased tendency to phase lock with increasing stimulation frequency, and this tendency was consistently larger than that of their regular counterparts (Figure 5E).
evidence: Analysis of phase locking across different stimulation frequencies with reference to Figure 5E.

claim: Spike-timing precision was strongly positively correlated with each measure of phase locking (R = 0.84, 0.87, and 0.7 using PLI1, PLI2, and PLI3, respectively; p≤0.001 in all cases).
source: Spike-timing precision was strongly positively correlated with each measure of phase locking (R = 0.84, 0.87, and 0.7 using PLI1, PLI2, and PLI3, respectively; p≤0.001 in all cases).
evidence: Correlation analysis between spike-timing precision and phase locking measures with statistical significance.

claim: Discriminability between different static head orientations was significantly higher for regular afferents than for irregular afferents across all angles (p<0.03 in all cases).
source: This finding was consistent across our population of otolith afferents as discriminability was significantly higher for regular afferents than for irregular afferents across all angles (Wilcoxon Ranksum test, p<0.03 in all cases; Figure 6B).
evidence: Statistical comparison of discriminability between afferent types using Wilcoxon Ranksum test.

claim: During natural everyday activities, the head moves with considerable linear acceleration (frequencies up to 20 Hz and amplitudes up to 8G).
source: Indeed, during natural everyday activities, the head not only moves with considerable linear acceleration (frequencies up to 20 Hz and amplitudes up to 8G; see Carriot et al., 2014 for human data and Carriot et al., 2017 for monkey and mouse data), but also frequently remains stationary during large periods of time (Carriot et al., 2014; Carriot et al., 2017).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to previous studies on head motion characteristics.

claim: Regular and irregular afferents display different morphological and physiological features.
source: Regular and irregular afferents further display different morphological and physiological features (reviewed in Goldberg, 2000, Cullen, 2012 and Eatock and Songer, 2011).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to review articles.

claim: Irregular otolith afferents show greater phase locking at higher frequencies (200–3,000 Hz) in response to sound and bone vibrations.
source: Interestingly, irregular otolith afferents show greater phase locking (i.e., firing only during a specific phase range of the sinusoidal stimulus) at higher frequencies (i.e., 200–3,000 Hz).
evidence: Statement based on previous studies of otolith afferent responses to sound and vibrations.

claim: Humans and monkeys can distinguish translational self-motion direction when the acceleration exceeds ~1 cm/s².
source: Behavioral studies have shown that humans and monkeys can distinguish translational self-motion direction when the acceleration exceeds ~1 cm/s2 (s MacNeilage et al., 2010, Soyka et al., 2011, Valko et al., 2012 and Bermúdez Rey et al., 2016; whereas those on monkeys include Gu et al., 2007 and Yu et al., 2015).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to behavioral studies.

claim: Neural detection thresholds for single otolith afferents are substantially higher (~10 cm/s²) than behavioral thresholds.
source: However, neural detection thresholds for single otolith afferents are substantially higher (~10 cm/s2) (Jamali et al., 2013; Yu et al., 2015), indicating that pooling the activities of multiple otolith afferents is required to give rise to perception of translational self-motion.
evidence: Comparison of neural thresholds from cited studies to behavioral thresholds, leading to inference about pooling.

claim: Single regular otolith afferents display discriminability values for static head orientation that are similar to those reported in psychophysical studies (~2°).
source: By contrast, when considering differences in static head orientation relative to gravity, our results here have shown that single regular otolith afferents display discriminability values that are similar to those reported in psychophysical studies (~2o) (Clemens et al., 2011; Valko et al., 2012; Karmali et al., 2014; Janssen et al., 2011; Dahlem et al., 2016; Tarnutzer et al., 2013).
evidence: Comparison of experimental results to psychophysical studies cited.

claim: Einstein's equivalence principle posits that the forces resulting from translational self-motion and changes in head orientation are physically indistinguishable from one another.
source: Einstein's equivalence principle posits that the forces resulting from both conditions are physically indistinguishable from one another (Angelaki and Cullen, 2008; Guedry, 1974; Young, 2011).
evidence: Statement of physical principle with supporting citations.

claim: Otolith afferents cannot be used alone to distinguish between translational self-motion and changes in head orientation.
source: Thus, otolith afferents, which sense linear acceleration, cannot be used alone to distinguish between both conditions (see Goldberg, 2012).
evidence: Logical inference from Einstein's equivalence principle with supporting citation.

claim: Semicircular canal afferents will be stimulated by the rotations associated with changing head orientation relative to gravity but not by translational self-motion.
source: It is important to note, however, that semicircular canal afferents will be stimulated by the rotations associated with changing head orientation relative to gravity but not by translational self-motion.
evidence: Statement based on known properties of semicircular canal afferents.

claim: The brain can theoretically distinguish between translational self-motion and changes in head orientation by integrating multi-sensory inputs from both otolith and canal afferents.
source: Accordingly, the brain can theoretically distinguish between these two movement conditions by integrating multi-sensory inputs from both otolith and canal afferents (Guedry, 1974; Young, 2011; Mayne, 1974; Angelaki and Yakusheva, 2009; Merfeld et al., 1999).
evidence: Theoretical inference supported by multiple citations.

claim: Purkinje cells in the caudal vermis integrate otolith and semicircular canal inputs.
source: Notably, Purkinje cells in the caudal vermis integrate otolith and semicircular canal inputs (reviewed in Angelaki and Cullen, 2008), such that one subset preferentially encodes translations (Yakusheva et al., 2007; Yakusheva et al., 2008) while another preferentially encodes tilts (Laurens et al., 2013).
evidence: Statement about neural integration supported by review and specific study citations.

claim: Translational self-motion at very low frequencies (<~0.1 Hz) is incorrectly interpreted as a change in head orientation, generating the 'somatogravic' illusion.
source: Interestingly, translational self-motion at very low frequencies (i.e., <~0.1 Hz) is incorrectly interpreted as a change in head orientation (Glasauer and Merfeld, 1997; Kaptein and Van Gisbergen, 2006; Seidman et al., 1998; Merfeld et al., 2005b; Merfeld et al., 2005a), thereby generating the 'somatogravic' illusion, a cause of disorientation that can be extremely dangerous for pilots.
evidence: Statement about perceptual illusion supported by multiple citations.

claim: Phase locking in auditory neurons is mediated by low-threshold voltage-gated potassium channels that promote hyperpolarization after spiking.
source: Such phase locking is mediated by low-threshold voltage-gated potassium channels that promote hyperpolarization after spiking (Oertel et al., 2000; Day et al., 2008; Kuznetsova et al., 2008; Rothman and Manis, 2003).
evidence: Statement about mechanism in auditory system supported by citations.

claim: Low-threshold voltage-gated potassium channels are present in vestibular afferents.
source: Interestingly, such channels are also present in vestibular afferents (Goldberg et al., 1984; Kalluri et al., 2010; Highstein and Politoff, 1978; Iwasaki et al., 2008), suggesting that the same mechanism mediates both phase locking and spike-timing precision in the auditory and vestibular systems.
evidence: Statement supported by citations to studies on vestibular afferents.

claim: Regular afferents integrate information from multiple hair cells located far away from the spike initiation zone.
source: Notably, regular afferents integrate information from multiple hair cells located far away from the spike initiation zone (Goldberg, 1991), whereas irregular afferents integrate synaptic input from relatively few hair cells and have their spike initiation zone located close by (Highstein and Politoff, 1978).
evidence: Statement about morphological differences supported by citations.

claim: Irregular afferents integrate synaptic input from relatively few hair cells and have their spike initiation zone located close by.
source: Notably, regular afferents integrate information from multiple hair cells located far away from the spike initiation zone (Goldberg, 1991), whereas irregular afferents integrate synaptic input from relatively few hair cells and have their spike initiation zone located close by (Highstein and Politoff, 1978).
evidence: Statement about morphological differences supported by citation.

claim: The configuration of irregular afferents (few hair cells, close spike initiation zone) probably minimizes spatial and temporal integration and is predicted to lead to more precise action potential firing.
source: The latter configuration probably minimizes spatial and temporal integration and is therefore predicted to lead to more precise action potential firing, consistent with our present findings.
evidence: Inference from morphological properties to functional consequences, consistent with experimental findings.

claim: The greater sensitivity of irregular canal afferents is not sufficient to compensate effectively for their higher resting discharge variability.
source: However, the greater sensitivity of irregular canal afferents is not sufficient to compensate effectively for their higher resting discharge variability (Sadeghi et al., 2007).
evidence: Statement about canal afferents supported by citation.

claim: Irregular canal afferents display lower detection thresholds than their regular counterparts over the entire behaviorally relevant frequency range.
source: Accordingly, irregular canal afferents display lower detection thresholds than their regular counterparts over the entire behaviorally relevant frequency range (Jamali et al., 2016; Massot et al., 2011; Sadeghi et al., 2007), while the detection thresholds of regular and irregular otolith afferents are similar over this range of frequencies (Jamali et al., 2013).
evidence: Comparison of canal and otolith afferents supported by citations.

claim: Regular canal afferents preferentially encode rotational self-motion through changes in firing rate, whereas irregular canal afferents preferentially encode these through precise spike timing.
source: Specifically, regular canal afferents preferentially encode rotational self-motion through changes in firing rate, whereas irregular canal afferents preferentially encode these through precise spike timing (Jamali et al., 2016).
evidence: Statement about canal afferent coding strategies supported by citation.

claim: Otolith afferents display sustained responses to static forces such as gravity.
source: In this context, it is important to note that while otolith afferents display sustained responses to static forces (such as gravity) (Angelaki and Dickman, 2000; Fernández and Goldberg, 1976a; Fernandez et al., 1972; Purcell et al., 2003), this is not the case for canal afferents as their sustained responses to rotations at constant angular velocities are minimal (Fernandez and Goldberg, 1971).
evidence: Comparison of otolith and canal afferent response properties supported by citations.

claim: Canal afferents' sustained responses to rotations at constant angular velocities are minimal.
source: In this context, it is important to note that while otolith afferents display sustained responses to static forces (such as gravity) (Angelaki and Dickman, 2000; Fernández and Goldberg, 1976a; Fernandez et al., 1972; Purcell et al., 2003), this is not the case for canal afferents as their sustained responses to rotations at constant angular velocities are minimal (Fernandez and Goldberg, 1971).
evidence: Statement about canal afferent properties supported by citation.

claim: Two male macaque monkeys (Macaca fascicularis), aged 6 and 8 years old, were used in the experiments.
source: Two male macaque monkeys (Macaca fascicularis), aged 6 and 8 years old, were prepared for chronic extracellular recording under aseptic conditions.
evidence: Direct statement of experimental subjects.

claim: CV* is a normalized coefficient of variation that is used to quantify resting discharge variability independently of differences in firing rate.
source: As detailed in the Materials and methods, CV* is a normalized coefficient of variation that is used to quantify resting discharge variability independently of differences in firing rate (Goldberg et al., 1984).
evidence: Definition of CV* measure with supporting citation.

claim: Firing rates during stimulation were not significantly different between regular (86 ± 5 spk/sec) and irregular (74 ± 7 spk/sec) afferents (p=0.16).
source: This difference in performance was not, however, due to differences in firing rates, either during stimulation (regular: 86 ± 5 spk/sec; irregular: 74 ± 7 spk/sec; p=0.16, Wilcoxon ranksum) or at rest (regular: 85 ± 5 spk/sec; irregular: 71 ± 6 spk/sec; p=0.19, Wilcoxon ranksum).
evidence: Statistical comparison of firing rates with Wilcoxon ranksum test showing no significant difference.

claim: Resting firing rates were not significantly different between regular (85 ± 5 spk/sec) and irregular (71 ± 6 spk/sec) afferents (p=0.19).
source: This difference in performance was not, however, due to differences in firing rates, either during stimulation (regular: 86 ± 5 spk/sec; irregular: 74 ± 7 spk/sec; p=0.16, Wilcoxon ranksum) or at rest (regular: 85 ± 5 spk/sec; irregular: 71 ± 6 spk/sec; p=0.19, Wilcoxon ranksum).
evidence: Statistical comparison of resting firing rates with Wilcoxon ranksum test showing no significant difference.

claim: Irregular otolith afferents with high sensitivity and resting discharge variability preferentially encode translational head motion over the 0.1–15 Hz frequency range.
source: Specifically, irregular otolith afferents with high sensitivity and resting discharge variability preferentially encode translational head motion over the 0.1–15 Hz frequency range, whereas regular otolith afferents with lower sensitivity and resting discharge variability instead preferentially encode static head orientation relative to gravity.
evidence: Summary conclusion based on multiple experimental findings presented in the study.

claim: Regular otolith afferents with lower sensitivity and resting discharge variability preferentially encode static head orientation relative to gravity.
source: Specifically, irregular otolith afferents with high sensitivity and resting discharge variability preferentially encode translational head motion over the 0.1–15 Hz frequency range, whereas regular otolith afferents with lower sensitivity and resting discharge variability instead preferentially encode static head orientation relative to gravity.
evidence: Summary conclusion based on multiple experimental findings presented in the study.

claim: The combined effects of greater sensitivity and resting discharge variability for irregular afferents enable greater information transmission via precise spike timing.
source: Specifically, our model suggests that the combined effects of the greater sensitivity and resting discharge variability for irregular afferents enable greater information transmission via precise spike timing.
evidence: Conclusion from mathematical modeling results.

claim: Pooling the activities of multiple otolith afferents is required to give rise to perception of translational self-motion.
source: However, neural detection thresholds for single otolith afferents are substantially higher (~10 cm/s2) (Jamali et al., 2013; Yu et al., 2015), indicating that pooling the activities of multiple otolith afferents is required to give rise to perception of translational self-motion.
evidence: Inference from comparison of single-neuron thresholds to behavioral thresholds, supported by citations.

claim: Little additional pooling of afferent activities is required for discrimination of static head orientation relative to gravity.
source: This suggests that little additional pooling of afferent activities is actually required.
evidence: Inference from comparison of single regular afferent discriminability to psychophysical performance.

claim: The exceptional sensitivity to static differences in spatial orientation serves an essential role in the maintenance of posture during everyday life.
source: We speculate that this exceptional sensitivity to static differences in spatial orientation serves an essential role in the maintenance of posture during everyday life.
evidence: Speculation about functional significance based on experimental findings.

claim: The same mechanism (low-threshold voltage-gated potassium channels) mediates both phase locking and spike-timing precision in the auditory and vestibular systems.
source: Interestingly, such channels are also present in vestibular afferents (Goldberg et al., 1984; Kalluri et al., 2010; Highstein and Politoff, 1978; Iwasaki et al., 2008), suggesting that the same mechanism mediates both phase locking and spike-timing precision in the auditory and vestibular systems.
evidence: Inference from presence of similar ion channels in both systems, supported by citations.

claim: Information transmission through the precise spike timing observed in irregular otolith afferents is tightly linked to their propensity to display phase locking in response to sinusoidal stimulation.
source: Thus, taken together, our results firmly establish that information transmission through the precise spike timing observed in irregular otolith afferents is tightly linked to their propensity to display phase locking in response to sinusoidal stimulation.
evidence: Conclusion based on correlation analysis between spike-timing precision and phase locking.

claim: Regular and irregular otolith afferents use different coding strategies to provide estimates of both dynamic head motion and static orientation relative to gravity.
source: Our results show that regular and irregular otolith afferents use different coding strategies to provide estimates of both dynamic head motion and static orientation relative to gravity.
evidence: Summary conclusion based on all experimental findings in the study.

claim: The information transmitted by regular afferents will become greater than that transmitted by irregular afferents as the frequency approaches zero.
source: Nonetheless, on the basis of our results obtained using static head orientations (i.e., 0 Hz), we predict that the information transmitted by regular afferents will become greater than that transmitted by irregular afferents as the frequency approaches zero (Figure 2E).
evidence: Prediction based on extrapolation from static orientation results.

claim: Regular afferents outperform their irregular counterparts at encoding low-frequency (i.e., <0.1 Hz) head acceleration signals.
source: This implies that regular afferents outperform their irregular counterparts at encoding low-frequency (i.e., <0.1 Hz) head acceleration signals.
evidence: Inference from predicted information transmission at low frequencies.

claim: Irregular otolith afferents will outperform their regular counterparts at encoding dynamic changes in head orientation, provided that their temporal frequency content is high enough (i.e., >0.1 Hz).
source: Specifically, we predict that irregular otolith afferents will outperform their regular counterparts at encoding dynamic changes in head orientation, provided that their temporal frequency content is high enough (i.e., >0.1 Hz).
evidence: Prediction based on experimental findings about frequency-dependent performance.

claim: Regular otolith afferents will outperform their irregular counterparts at encoding low frequency (i.e., <0.1 Hz) translational self-motion.
source: Moreover, we predict that regular otolith afferents will outperform their irregular counterparts at encoding low frequency (i.e., <0.1 Hz) translational self-motion.
evidence: Prediction based on experimental findings about frequency-dependent performance.

claim: The trial-to-trial variability during static stimulation will be proportional to the resting discharge variability, and thus lower for regular afferents relative to their irregular counterparts.
source: As a result, the trial-to-trial variability during static stimulation will be proportional to the resting discharge variability, and thus lower for regular afferents relative to their irregular counterparts.
evidence: Inference based on the absence of strong nonlinearities during static stimulation.

claim: The lower resting discharge variability of regular afferents offsets the detrimental effects of lower sensitivity, thereby giving rise to greater stimulus discrimination for static head orientations.
source: Our results show that this lower resting discharge variability offsets the detrimental effects of lower sensitivity, thereby giving rise to greater stimulus discrimination.
evidence: Explanation of mechanism based on experimental results.

claim: Theory predicts that trial-to-trial variability during stimulation will increase with increasing resting discharge variability for linear systems.
source: Thus, while theory predicts that trial-to-trial variability during stimulation will increase with increasing resting discharge variability for linear systems (Chacron et al., 2003; Risken, 1996), this is not valid when strong response nonlinearities are present, as is the case during naturalistic translational self-motion.
evidence: Statement of theoretical prediction with supporting citations.

claim: The relatively lower intensity stimuli resulting from statically positioning the head at different orientations relative to gravity do not elicit strong response nonlinearities from either regular or irregular afferents.
source: Nevertheless, it is important to note that the relatively lower intensity stimuli resulting from statically positioning the head at different orientations relative to gravity do not elicit strong response nonlinearities from either regular or irregular afferents (Fernandez et al., 1972).
evidence: Statement about response properties supported by citation.

claim: High-frequency stimuli (sound and vibration) cause fluid pressure waves in vestibular end organs, which in turn activate vestibular hair cells.
source: It has been proposed that such high-frequency stimuli cause fluid pressure waves in vestibular end organs, which in turn activate vestibular hair cells (Eatock and Songer, 2011; Curthoys and Grant, 2015).
evidence: Statement of proposed mechanism with supporting citations.

claim: The strong correlation between spike-timing precision in response to naturalistic stimulation and phase locking to sinusoidal stimulation suggests that these two processes share common underlying mechanisms.
source: The strong correlation between spike-timing precision in response to naturalistic stimulation and phase locking to sinusoidal stimulation seen for otolith afferents suggests that these two processes share common underlying mechanisms.
evidence: Inference from observed correlation in experimental data.

claim: Neurons in the auditory system display precise spike timing, which is commonly associated with phase locking.
source: Neurons in the auditory system also display precise spike timing, which is commonly associated with phase locking (see recent review by Heil and Peterson, 2017).
evidence: Statement about auditory system supported by citation to review.

claim: The firing rate modulation of tilt-sensitive cerebellar Purkinje cells appears to provide a neural substrate for the somatogravic illusion.
source: The firing rate modulation of tilt-sensitive cerebellar Purkinje cells appears to provide a neural substrate for this perceptual effect (Laurens et al., 2013).
evidence: Statement about neural substrate supported by citation.

claim: Parietoinsular vestibular cortex neurons can discriminate tilts from translations.
source: Parietoinsular vestibular cortex neurons can likewise discriminate tilts from translations (Liu et al., 2011).
evidence: Statement about cortical neurons supported by citation.

claim: All experimental protocols were approved by the McGill University Animal Care Committee (#2001–4096) and were in compliance with the guidelines of the Canadian Council on Animal Care.
source: All experimental protocols were approved by the McGill University Animal Care Committee (#2001–4096) and were in compliance with the guidelines of the Canadian Council on Animal Care.
evidence: Statement of ethical approval.
